---
title: "Reverse-KL intrinsic reward for prior sampling"
description: "An alternative intrinsic-reward formulation that optimizes the behavioral sampling policy by minimizing reverse KL on latent marginals."
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- As an alternative to the trajectory-level vanilla BPO formulation in the
  [computational model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd), the
  intrinsic policy can be trained via reinforcement learning with a step-wise
  intrinsic reward defined over policy-induced latent marginals.
- Maximizing the expected intrinsic reward under the intrinsic policy minimizes
  reverse KL divergence from its latent marginal to the single-sample
  variance-optimal importance proposal for the perceptual prior gradient, though
  reverse KL alone does not enforce support coverage or guarantee lower variance
  under restricted policy classes.
- Because the ratio of extrinsic to intrinsic latent marginals is unknown, this
  approach requires estimating that density ratio—for instance via
  least-squares importance fitting with running feature averages from extrinsic
  trajectories—and estimation error affects both the reward and the prior
  update.
:::

## Relation to the parent model

In the [computational model of aesthetics](computational-aesthetics.qmd), the
extrinsically motivated policy $\pi_e$ optimizes ordinary task return and
determines the latent distribution that the perceptual prior $R_\theta$ should
predict, while the intrinsically motivated policy $\pi_i$ acts as the behavioral
policy collecting samples to estimate the prior gradient. The parent page's
primary candidate model optimizes $\pi_i$ using trajectory-level vanilla
[behavioral policy optimization (BPO)](behavioral-policy-optimization.qmd)
[@papini2024], which minimizes forward KL via weighted cross-entropy over full
trajectories using known action-probability ratios.

This page develops an alternative formulation that operates on single-step
latent marginals $p_\pi(z)$ instead of trajectory distributions and trains
$\pi_i$ with an explicit intrinsic reward $r_I(z)$.

## Candidate reward: selecting efficient learning samples

For either policy $\pi \in \{\pi_e,\pi_i\}$, let $p_\pi(z)$ be the marginal
distribution of a latent sampled along its trajectory. For example, run the
policy for a fixed number of transitions and sample one transition uniformly.
Use the same time weighting and initial conditions for both policies. Hold
$\pi_e$, the fixed encoder $F$, and the current prior parameters $\theta$ fixed
when comparing intrinsic policies.

The target loss and the gradient contributed by one latent are

$$
  L(\theta)=\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}[-\log R_\theta(Z)],\qquad
  g_\theta(z)=\nabla_\theta[-\log R_\theta(z)].
$$

For a latent from an intrinsic trajectory, the importance-weighted estimate is

$$
  \widehat g(Z)=w(Z)g_\theta(Z),\qquad
  w(z)=\frac{p_{\pi_e}(z)}{p_{\pi_i}(z)}.
$$

The denominator measures how often $\pi_i$ encounters the latent across its
trajectory. If $\pi_i$ samples wherever $p_{\pi_e}(z)g_\theta(z)$ is nonzero,
then $\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}\widehat g=\nabla_\theta L$. Among unrestricted
proposals, the one minimizing the sum of the component variances of this
single-sample estimate is [@alain2016, Theorem 1]

$$
  q_\theta^*(z)=\frac{p_{\pi_e}(z)\|g_\theta(z)\|_2}{C_\theta},\qquad
  C_\theta=\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}\|g_\theta(Z)\|_2.
$$

Assume $0<C_\theta<\infty$ and finite estimator second moments. Relative to
their frequency under $\pi_e$, latents that give larger prior gradients should
be sampled more often.

**Why reverse KL?** Vanilla BPO fits the behavioral policy using forward KL from
the optimal proposal to the behavioral distribution. Reversing those arguments
places the expectation under the policy collecting the rewards. On an intrinsic
trajectory, assign each observed latent the reward

$$
  r_I(z)=\log\|g_\theta(z)\|_2
       +\log\frac{p_{\pi_e}(z)}{p_{\pi_i}(z)}.
$$

Its expected trajectory average is

$$
  \mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[r_I(Z)]
  =\log C_\theta-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\pi_i}\Vert q_\theta^*).
$$

Thus maximizing intrinsic reward minimizes reverse KL. When choosing a sampling
policy, require it to cover every region that contributes to the target
gradient. Reverse KL alone does not enforce this: a policy can earn finite
expected reward while never visiting such a region, leaving its prior-gradient
estimate biased. If an available policy can realize $q_\theta^*$, it attains the
single-sample variance optimum. Otherwise, a smaller reverse KL need not imply
smaller variance. The result also does not account for correlations between
successive prior updates.

## Candidate estimator: running latent feature averages {#sec-feature-ema}

The two marginals need not be estimated separately. Least-squares importance
fitting [@kanamori2009, sec. 2.2] estimates their ratio by minimizing

$$
  \mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[w(Z)^2]
                   -\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}[w(Z)].
$$

When the target marginal is supported by the sampling marginal and their ratio
has finite second moment, this differs from the mean squared error under
$p_{\pi_i}$ by a constant and a factor of one half.

For a feature model $w_\eta(z)=\eta^\top f(z)$, maintain an exponential moving
average $m_e$ of the fixed features $f(z)$ **from extrinsic trajectories only**.
Then $\eta^\top m_e$ estimates the second expectation; intrinsic trajectory
samples supply the first. For example, one-hot features retain category
frequencies, whereas the mean of a continuous latent alone cannot distinguish
two distributions with the same mean but different tails.

On an intrinsic trajectory, use the pre-update ratio estimate in two ways: add
$\log w_\eta(z)$ to the log gradient norm for the reward, and multiply
$g_\theta(z)$ by $w_\eta(z)$ for the prior update. The logarithms require
positive weights and gradient norms for finite rewards. Restricting the feature
model to positive ratios or flooring estimates for numerical stability can
introduce approximation error. Limited features, correlated samples, and changes
in either policy can also make the estimated weights inaccurate.

## Open questions

- **Importance ratio:** for the feature EMA candidate, which fixed features,
  positivity constraints, and learning timescales yield accurate weights? How
  much bias arises from correlated experience and marginal drift, and when does
  weighting outperform unweighted prior learning?
- **KL and gradient variance:** sharing a global optimum does not guarantee that
  gradient-estimator variance increases monotonically with
  $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\pi_i}\Vert q_\theta^*)$. Under what additional conditions
  does reducing this KL reduce variance and improve learning? Restrictions on
  attainable latent distributions can also make the KL-optimal and
  variance-optimal policies differ.
- **RL nonstationarity:** how should the RL time horizon and update schedule
  handle an intrinsic reward $r_I(z)$ that changes with both $\theta$ and the
  marginal ratio $p_{\pi_e}(z)/p_{\pi_i}(z)$?
